results.title: Naval architecture - Metacentric Stability, Buoyancy, Stability | Britannica
excerpts:
Metacentric stability
in
naval architecture
If the centre of gravity of the ship is too high, the righting moment for any inclination is negative; that is, it acts to incline the ship still further. The ship then has transverse metacentric instability.
The distance GM for positive stability, known as the metacentric height, is taken as one index of the degree of metacentric stability. The other is the range of stability, or the angle of inclination at which the metacentric height diminishes to zero.
For inclinations beyond this the metacentric height becomes negative, the righting moment becomes a capsizing moment and the ship rolls over.
A greater range of metacentric stability can be built into a ship by raising the uppermost watertight deck to a higher position above the calm-water plane of flotation.
For fishing vessels it may have two values, one for the outgoing and one for the return or loaded part of the voyage. The range of positive transverse GM for a normal ship to run in the open sea is usually in excess of 40° and may run as high as 70° or more, provided the hull remains intact and the weights do not shift.

results.title: Metacentric height - Wikipedia
excerpts:
Metacentric height - Wikipedia
It is calculated as the distance between the centre of gravity of a ship and its metacentre. A larger metacentric height implies greater initial stability against overturning.
